Grade 4 · Unit 4.1

Energy, Speed, and Collisions

How can we use speed, collisions, heat, light, and sound as evidence that energy moves?

Look for the tags AnalogyDiagramTry itDataReal world

  • 1 Speed and energy

  • 3 Heat moves from warmer to cooler

  • 5 Try it at home

Concept 1

Speed and energy

Faster moving objects can cause bigger changes, which is evidence that they have more energy.

Analogy

Rolling ball

a slow ball and a fast ball hitting small blocks.

“A fast ball can knock things over more.”

Try it

Ramp and car

a toy car released from a low ramp and a high ramp.

“Higher ramp, faster car, farther push.”

Data

Distance moved

a simple bar graph of block movement for low ramp and high ramp, plus a real observation log.

“The faster car moved the block farther. Real log: record your low-ramp and high-ramp trials. Provided dataset: low ramp 2 cm, 2 cm, 3 cm; high ramp 7 cm, 8 cm, 8 cm.”

Real world

Sledding on a Michigan hill

a sled going down a snowy hill.

“A faster sled can push farther into the snow.”

Concept 2

Collisions change energy

When objects collide, motion energy can move, so things can speed up, slow down, or change shape.

Try it

Marble target

a marble rolling into a small block target.

“Roll the marble. Watch the target move. Energy moved.”

Diagram

Before and after collision

marble before contact, block after contact, arrows showing motion.

“Before: marble moves. After: block moves. Energy changed places.”

Data

Predict-test table

columns for Prediction, Test, What happened.

“Ask: What if the marble is faster? What if it is heavier? Predict, then test.”

Real world

Bumper cars

two bumper cars touching and changing direction.

“Collisions can change speed and direction.”

Concept 3

Heat moves from warmer to cooler

Heat energy transfers from warmer objects to cooler objects until temperatures become more equal.

Analogy

Hot cocoa and spoon

a spoon in a cup of warm cocoa.

“The spoon gets warm. Heat moved from cocoa to spoon.”

Try it

Cup warming

hands wrapped around a warm cup. Adult handles warm water.

“Your hands warm up because heat moves into them.”

Data

Temperature change table

warm water cooling over time, with a real observation log and provided dataset.

“Warm things cool down. Heat leaves them. Real log: start, 5 minutes, 10 minutes. Provided dataset: 40°C, 37°C, 35°C.”

Real world

Michigan winter coat

a child wearing a coat.

“A coat slows heat leaving your body. It does not make heat.”

Concept 4

Sound and light can move energy

Sound vibrations and light can also transfer energy to other things.

Try it

Sound moves rice

rice on plastic wrap over a cup or near a speaker; the rice jumps when sound is made.

“Make a sound. Watch rice jump. Sound moved energy.”

Try it

Light warms a hand

a hand held near a lamp, not touching it. Adult handles the warm lamp.

“Hold your hand near the lamp. It feels warm. Light moved energy.”

Data

Energy-transfer chart

columns for heat, light, sound, and observed change.

“Heat warmed the spoon. Light warmed the hand. Sound moved rice.”

Real world

Sunlight on snow

sunlight shining on a snowy yard.

“Sunlight can melt snow. Light energy changes things.”

Hands-on · Design or investigate

Try it at home or in class

Fair-test task: “Which collision makes the target move farthest?” Students choose one variable to change, such as marble speed or marble mass. They keep the target the same, predict outcomes, test three times, graph results, and write one evidence sentence.

Try it

What you need

toy car or marble, cardboard ramp, books, small block or target, paper cups, spoon, warm water, thermometer if available, flashlight or lamp, plastic wrap, rubber band, small speaker or drum, rice, paper, pencil, tape.

Safety: adult handles warm water and warm lamps; do not stare into bright lights; keep water away from Chromebooks.

Try it

What you do

Test ramp height and block movement. Run marble collisions and predict outcomes. Observe heat transfer with a warm cup. Observe sound moving rice and light warming a hand. Record real observations.

No time or no good weather? Use this data

This data is a backup. It lets you practice reading evidence, but the standard expects you to collect your own when you can.

if the investigation cannot be run, use ramp data low ramp 2 cm, 2 cm, 3 cm; high ramp 7 cm, 8 cm, 8 cm; cooling data 40°C, 37°C, 35°C.

Near you: Great Lakes winter: heat loss from buildings, snow reflecting sunlight, and sound traveling across cold air. A faster sled can push farther into a snowbank.

Words to know

energy
the ability to cause change.
speed
how fast something moves.
collision
when objects hit each other.
transfer
to move from one place or object to another.
heat transfer
energy moving from warmer to cooler.
vibration
quick back-and-forth motion.
sound
energy from vibrations.
light
energy we can see.
predict
say what you think will happen next.
evidence
observations or data that support a claim.
Tutor notes: misconceptions, standards, pacing

Pacing: five 30-minute sessions.

Common misconceptions to listen for:

  • “Faster objects have less energy.” Correct: faster objects usually have more energy.
  • “Energy disappears in a collision.” Correct: energy can transfer and change motion.
  • “Cold flows into things.” Correct: heat transfers from warmer to cooler.
  • “A coat makes heat.” Correct: a coat slows heat leaving your body.
  • “Sound cannot move things.” Correct: sound vibrations can move small objects.
  • “Still things have no energy.” Correct: energy can be present or transferring even when the evidence is subtle.

Limits and cautions:

  • 4-PS3-2 is only partly earned here; electric current is intentionally deferred to 4.2.
  • Grade 4 does not require kinetic-energy formulas; the unit uses speed evidence only.
  • Sound-moving-rice can be subtle; the provided dataset guarantees evidence if equipment fails.
  • Temperature measurement is optional; the key idea is direction of heat transfer, not exact scales.

Michigan Science Standards this unit earns:

  • 4-PS3-1: Use evidence to relate the speed of an object to its energy.
  • 4-PS3-3: Ask questions and make predictions about changes in energy transferred when objects collide.
  • 4-PS3-2: Observe that energy can be transferred by sound, light, heat, and electric currents.

Connections: Builds on: Unit 0: How Science Works; K-A Pushes and Pulls; 3.1 Forces, Motion, and Magnets. Builds toward: Unit 8.1 Contact Forces & Collisions; Unit 2 Thermal Energy; Unit 8.2 Energy Transformation & Conservation.
